raw_response:
I am 69 years old and have been farming these fields for over 50 years. I only finished primary school, so I do not read those agricultural bulletins or calculate fancy formulas. I watch what my neighbors do, remember what worked last year, and decide how much I can afford to spend.

My wheat is already in the ground from last October. I planted about 30 jin of improved seed per mu on my 6 mu of land, and the seedlings look decent this spring. Right now the wheat is at jointing stage, so I need to top-dress with urea and irrigate soon. I will put down roughly half a bag of urea per mu — that is about 25 kilos — which should give the wheat enough nitrogen to fill out the heads. In total, counting the compound fertilizer I spread last autumn before sowing, I figure I am using about 15–18 kilos of actual nitrogen per mu, plus some phosphorus and potassium from the compound bag. I will irrigate four times in total this wheat season, including the winter irrigation I already did and the two more times the crop will need before harvest in early June. I also spray pesticides three times — once for weeds and a couple more times if I see aphids or rust.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize on the same 6 mu. Everyone around here uses hybrid maize seed now — you cannot get good yield without it — so I will buy Denghai or Nongda hybrid seed, about 1.5 packages per mu. I am getting too old to turn the soil deeply twice in one month, and the window between wheat harvest and maize planting is only a few days, so I will plant without tillage, just drilling the seed straight into the wheat stubble. For fertilizer, I will spread compound fertilizer at planting and maybe side-dress a little urea when the maize is knee-high. Total nitrogen will be a bit less than the wheat, around 16 kilos per mu, because maize does not need as much fuss if the rains cooperate. I will irrigate three times if the weather stays dry, and spray pesticides twice — mainly herbicide and once for corn borer.

I keep some money aside for my grandchildren’s school fees, so I cannot afford to buy the most expensive inputs. But I also know that cutting too much on fertilizer is risky — last year my neighbor tried saving on urea and his wheat was thin and yellow. I would rather spend a little more and sleep soundly.
